questions.question: What does it mean when a building or system is “built to code”?

answers.text: It is guaranteed to be 100% free of risk.
answers.feedback: Building to code means meeting the minimum legal threshold of tolerable risk—not achieving zero risk or best-in-class construction.

answers.text: It represents the highest quality of design and construction available.
answers.feedback: Building to code means meeting the minimum legal threshold of tolerable risk—not achieving zero risk or best-in-class construction.

answers.text: It meets the minimum legal standard for tolerable risk.
answers.feedback: Making a structure completely risk-free would be practically and economically impossible. Instead, a code defines the minimum legal baseline required to limit unacceptable risk.

answers.text: It follows recommended industry guidelines that are optional to enforce.
answers.feedback: Building to code means meeting the minimum legal threshold of tolerable risk—not achieving zero risk or best-in-class construction.

questions.question: A new edition of the National Building Code of Canada is published today. Can a local official enforce its new rules tomorrow?

answers.text: Yes—a National Model Code becomes law across Canada as soon as it is published.
answers.feedback: A National Model Code carries zero legal force on its own. It only becomes enforceable after a province or territory adopts it through its own legislation.

answers.text: No—a National Model Code has no legal force until a province or territory adopts it into law.
answers.feedback: A National Model Code is a technical blueprint, not a law. Under Canada’s Constitution, only provinces and territories have the legal authority to adopt codes into enforceable legislation.

answers.text: Yes—if the new requirement addresses an immediate safety hazard.

answers.text: No—each municipality must write its own building code from scratch.
